title: Where the Chain Loop Begins
statement:
A singly linked list is laid out in an array. The nodes are numbered 0 … n − 1, and next[i] is the node that follows node i, or -1 if node i points to nothing. So next[i] plays the role of node i's .next pointer, and -1 is null.

The head is node 0. Walk from it by following next. If the walk reaches -1, return -1. If it runs into a loop, return the number of the first node of the loop: the first node on the walk that you would visit a second time.

Nodes that cannot be reached from node 0 are not part of the list. Ignore them.

Aim for O(1) extra memory, and treat next like real pointers: do not use n to decide when to stop.

examples.why: 0 → 1 → 2 → 3 → 4 → 2. Nodes 0 and 1 are the lead-in; node 2 is where the circle closes.
0 → 2 → 1 → 0. The whole list is a loop, so the head itself is the entry.
0 → 3 → 2 → end. Node 1 points at itself, but it cannot be reached from the head.

hints: Detecting that a loop exists is the classic fast and slow pointer trick. Once they meet, what do you know about the distances involved?
Let the lead-in have length a. When slow and fast meet, slow has walked some distance d and fast has walked 2d, and the difference d is a whole number of laps.
After the meeting, put one pointer back on the head and leave the other at the meeting node. Step both one node at a time; they meet exactly at the loop entry.

explain.intuition:
A walk from the head either ends at -1 or is shaped like the letter ρ: a straight lead-in of a nodes, then a loop of length L. A set of visited nodes finds the entry directly (the first repeat), but costs O(n) memory.

Floyd's method needs two pointers. Run slow one step and fast two steps until they meet. At that moment fast has walked exactly twice as far as slow, and the extra distance is a whole number of laps, so slow's distance d is a multiple of L. Now start a new pointer at the head and keep one at the meeting point, both moving one step. After a steps the new pointer stands on the entry. The other one has walked d + a in total from the head, which is a plus whole laps, so it is also on the entry. They meet there for the first time.
steps: While fast and next[fast] are not -1: move slow one step and fast two steps. If they are equal, stop.
If fast ran off the end, return -1.
Set p = 0. While p !== slow, move both p and slow one step.
pitfalls: Returning the meeting node. Fast and slow meet somewhere inside the loop, not necessarily at its start: in [1, 2, 3, 4, 2] they meet at node 3, but the entry is node 2.
Checking slow === fast before the first move. Both start at the head, so the check fires immediately.
Assuming the loop goes back to the head. In most inputs it closes somewhere in the middle.

solutions.title: Remember visited nodes
solutions.idea: Walk from the head and keep a set of visited nodes. The first node you see twice is the entry.

solutions.title: Floyd: meet, then restart from the head
solutions.idea: Fast and slow meet inside the loop. A pointer from the head and a pointer from the meeting node, moving together, meet at the entry.

followups: How would you compute the length of the loop once you have the meeting point?
The same idea finds a repeated value in an array of n + 1 numbers from 1 to n without changing the array. How does that array become a linked list?
